text: EverQuest II is a 3D fantasy massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG) originally developed and published by Sony Online Entertainment for Microsoft Windows PCs and released in November 2004. It serves as a sequel to the original EverQuest, which was released five years earlier, and includes updated graphics, more streamlined gameplay, and an abundance of voice acting featuring actors such as Christopher Lee, Heather Graham, Minnie Driver, Wil Wheaton, Dwight Schultz, Richard Horvitz, Alan Dale, and Danica McKellar. According to SOE, the game featured 130 hours of spoken dialog recorded by 266 voice actors in October 2004, with additional dialog added through updates, including player voice emotes introduced in September 2005 via the Desert of Flames expansion. The music, composed by Emmy-award-winning Laura Karpman and recorded by the FILMharmonic Orchestra Prague, spans over ninety minutes and features unique themes for each location, aiming for a cinematic feel; the expansions Echoes of Faydwer and Rise of Kunark include themes from the original EverQuest arranged by Inon Zur, and Rise of Kunark introduced a new combat music system with 14 contextual themes based on enemy strength and battle tide. The game is set in an alternate future 500 years after the original EverQuest's events, functioning as a parallel universe that diverges at the conclusion of the Planes of Power expansion, allowing both games to develop independently without interfering with each other. Characters and locations from the original are altered by centuries of war and destruction, and players can access familiar places and characters through "heritage items" obtained via heritage quests. Each player creates a character in the 3D world of Norrath, choosing from races such as human, barbarian, dwarf, erudite, ogre, iksar, troll, gnome, half elf, high elf, halfling, Vah Shir, wood elf, dark elf, Kerra, Ratonga, Sarnak, Fae, and Arasai, with the Froglok race initially locked until a server-wide quest was completed. Players select one of four archetypes—Fighter, Scout, Priest, or Mage—and choose a class at level 10 and a subclass at level 20, though this system changed in 2006 so that the final class is selected at character creation. Characters gain experience through quests, exploration, and monster kills, with no experience loss or level loss upon death; instead, they respawn with full gear at revival locations, though a minor experience debt is repaid, and gear degrades after 10 consecutive deaths, requiring repair for a fee. The game emphasizes quests, with over 6,000 existing, and supports player interaction through grouping (up to six players), raids (up to 24), voice chat, mail, global chat, a marketplace, and tools like "looking-for-group" and "looking-for-work." Guilds are central to gameplay, with experience bars and levels up to 150 earned primarily through "writs" and killing epic monsters, unlocking rewards such as housing, mounts, house items, apparel, titles, guild halls, and a hosted website with forum and bank features. Guild recruitment tools are integrated, and players can maintain houses. A secure commission system allows players to sell crafting skills or use the common market to sell finished items. The game originally operated on a subscription model, but in July 2010, a free-to-play version called EverQuest II Extended was released on a separate server, funded by microtransactions or optional subscriptions. By November 2011, the subscription service was fully cancelled, transitioning all servers to free-to-play with microtransactions as the revenue stream. In February 2005, the game partnered with Pizza Hut, allowing players to order pizza via the "/pizza" chat command, a promotion that ended but generated significant press. In June 2005, Station Exchange—an official auction system on designated servers—was introduced, and in December 2008, Station Cash, a real-money trading (RMT) feature, was added. In January 2009, EverQuest II became available on Steam through a collaboration with Valve. In March 2006, SOE ended its Chinese and Korean operations for EverQuest II, which were managed by Gamania, with beta access ending on March 29 and all accounts moved to US servers by March 30. In October 2012, Krono was introduced as a real-money purchase option that grants 30 days of Gold subscription and can be traded or gifted, offering a safer alternative to purchasing SC cards. The game was nominated for "Best Massively Multiplayer Online Game" at GameSpot's 2004 awards and runner-up for "Best Persistent World Game" at IGN's 2004 awards, both losing to World of Warcraft. It was named the seventh-best computer game of 2004 by Computer Games Magazine and won "Most Improved Game" at GameSpy's 2006 awards for the addition of PvP servers and the Echoes of Faydwer expansion. After adopting free-to-play in 2011, it won "Best Bang for the Buck" at Massively's annual awards. EverQuest II reached 100,000 active accounts within 24 hours of release and grew to over 300,000 in January 2005, with a subscriber peak of 325,000 in 2005. As of September 2020, it had 21,000 subscribers and 29,000 monthly active players. EverQuest II: East, an alternate edition for East Asia, was developed by Sony Online Entertainment and launched in April 2005, featuring localized tutorials, a separate "SOGA Model" character design, and proprietary missions, but failed due to poor localization; Gamania terminated its operations on March 29, 2006, and all Chinese, Taiwanese, and Korean accounts were transferred to US servers. In February 2015, Sony Computer Entertainment sold Sony Online Entertainment to investment company Inception Acquisitions, which rebranded the studio as Daybreak Game Company, which continues to develop and publish EverQuest II. The game has been used in academic studies to analyze virtual economic behavior, with findings showing real-world patterns in production, consumption, and money supply, and that less than one percent (0.43%) of players are Platinum Farmers, with over 77% of them being Chinese. It received mostly positive reviews, earning an 83 out of 100 average on Metacritic, with critics noting it as more convenient and forgiving than the original, though less groundbreaking, with its extensive voice acting being a major advancement. While praised for its presentation and photorealistic graphics, performance issues were common on higher settings, requiring powerful systems for optimal play. The game's expansions, including Tears of Veeshan (which includes Chains of Eternity), introduce new zones, features, creatures, items, and player races, with access to levels above 92 requiring the purchase of Tears of Veeshan. Free-to-play accounts have access to the same areas as subscription accounts but face restrictions such as limited bag slots, coin limits, quest journal limits, race and class restrictions, and gear limitations, though many restrictions have been removed, including the inability to buy or sell items on the broker, spell tier limits, and the alternate advancement slider. The game's feature set has expanded since its 2004 release, including the introduction of Adventure Packs—smaller digital expansions with plot lines, zones, creatures, and items—though the development team now releases free zones and content instead. Expansions are available through retail or digital download and often include bonus features like in-game creatures. EverQuest II: East used similar settings to the original, with localized content and local language character naming, but most dialogue remained in English except for the novice tutorial, which was localized by Gamania.
